specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe: different levels of organisation in an ecosystem from individual organisms to the whole ecosystem; the importance of interdependence and competition in a community.

Students should be able to, when provided with appropriate information: suggest the factors for which organisms are competing in a given habitat; suggest how organisms are adapted to the conditions in which they live.
An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there.
Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.

Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community. This is called interdependence. A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
Students should be able to extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables relating to the interaction of organisms within a community.
Students should be able to explain how a change in an abiotic factor would affect a given community given appropriate data or context.

Abiotic (non-living) factors which can affect a community are: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals.
Students should be able to extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables relating to the effect of abiotic factors on organisms within a community.
Students should be able to explain how a change in a biotic factor might affect a given community given appropriate data or context.

Biotic (living) factors which can affect a community are: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another so the numbers are no longer sufficient to breed.
Students should be able to extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables relating to the effect of biotic factors on organisms within a community.
Students should be able to explain how organisms are adapted to live in their natural environment, given appropriate information.
Organisms have features (adaptations) that enable them to survive in the conditions in which they normally live. These adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional.

Some organisms live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. These organisms are called extremophiles. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

concepts.definition: The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
The place where an organism lives. It supplies the conditions and the materials the organism needs from its surroundings in order to survive and reproduce.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat. A population is the level of organisation between the individual organism and the community.
The populations of all the different species living together in a habitat. Within a community each species depends on the other species living there.

Organisms of the same or different species competing for the same resource where the supply is limited. Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.
Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community.
A community where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.

A non-living factor which can affect a community. The abiotic factors are: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals.

A living factor which can affect a community. The biotic factors are: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another so the numbers are no longer sufficient to breed.
A feature that an organism has which enables it to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

The three types of adaptation. Structural adaptations are features of the organism's body, such as its shape or covering. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does. Functional adaptations are the ways processes inside the organism's body work.
An organism that lives in an environment that is very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

concepts.term: Materials required to survive and reproduce
concepts.definition: To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there, for example light, water and mineral ions for a plant, and food from other organisms for an animal.

misconceptions.question: Is an ecosystem the same thing as the community of organisms living in an area?
misconceptions.correct: No. A community is the living organisms; an ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
misconceptions.misconception: A community and an ecosystem are the same thing, so a community is made up of both the living organisms and the non-living (abiotic) parts of the habitat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words are used loosely in everyday language to mean 'the wildlife of a place', and pictures of ecosystems usually label only the plants and animals, leaving the soil, water, light and temperature unlabelled.
misconceptions.correction: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment, so the abiotic parts of the habitat are part of the ecosystem but are not part of the community.

misconceptions.question: Do plants compete with each other for the same things that animals compete for?
misconceptions.correct: No. Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil, while animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants compete with each other for food, mates and territory, in the same way that animals do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Competition is usually taught first using animal examples, and students often call the mineral ions a plant takes from the soil its 'food' rather than materials the plant uses to make its own food.
misconceptions.correction: Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.

misconceptions.question: In a stable community, do the population sizes stay exactly the same?
misconceptions.correct: No. A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
misconceptions.misconception: A stable community is one in which nothing changes at all: the population sizes stay exactly the same and the species stop competing with each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'stable' is heard as 'fixed', and predator and prey graphs are often summarised as 'balanced' without students noticing that the lines keep rising and falling around an average.
misconceptions.correction: In a stable community all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant. Numbers still rise and fall, and the species still compete for resources and still depend on each other.

misconceptions.question: If one species in a community is removed, which species are affected?
misconceptions.correct: The whole community can be affected, because within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc.
misconceptions.misconception: A change that affects one species affects that species alone, or at most the species that feeds directly on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Food chains are drawn as single lines, so students follow the effect one step along the chain and stop, instead of thinking about all the ways species depend on each other.
misconceptions.correction: Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. This is called interdependence, so if one species is removed it can affect the whole community.

misconceptions.question: Is a new predator arriving in a habitat an abiotic factor?
misconceptions.correct: No. A new predator arriving is a biotic (living) factor. The abiotic (non-living) factors are light intensity, temperature, moisture levels, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity and direction, carbon dioxide levels for plants, and oxygen levels for aquatic animals.
misconceptions.misconception: Students cannot reliably tell biotic from abiotic factors: they may label a living influence such as a new predator arriving as an abiotic factor, or label a non-living factor such as dissolved oxygen as a biotic factor.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'environmental factor' as meaning 'non-living', so every outside influence, including other organisms, gets labelled abiotic.
misconceptions.correction: Abiotic factors are the non-living factors: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals. Biotic factors are the living ones: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another.

misconceptions.question: Can something an organism does count as an adaptation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Organisms have features (adaptations) that enable them to survive in the conditions in which they normally live, and these adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional.
misconceptions.misconception: Only parts of the body are adaptations; the way an organism behaves is just behaviour and does not count as an adaptation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adaptation is nearly always introduced with pictures of body parts such as thick fur, large ears or long roots, so structural examples dominate what students remember.
misconceptions.correction: Adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional. A behaviour such as resting in shade in the heat of the day enables the organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives, so it is an adaptation.

misconceptions.question: What makes an organism an extremophile?
misconceptions.correct: Extremophiles live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.
misconceptions.misconception: Extremophiles are organisms that put up with extreme conditions for short periods, and extreme conditions means very hot conditions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The best known examples are heat-loving bacteria, and stories about animals surviving harsh weather blur the difference between briefly tolerating conditions and normally living in them.
misconceptions.correction: Extremophiles live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles, living permanently in water that is both very hot and under very high pressure.

misconceptions.question: Do plants need materials from other living organisms?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants make their own food, so they do not depend on any other living organisms to survive and reproduce.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Photosynthesis is taught as the plant 'making its own food', which students extend into complete independence, overlooking that within a community each species depends on other species for pollination and seed dispersal.
misconceptions.correction: To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there. Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc., so plants are part of that interdependence too.

misconceptions.question: Is a community all the organisms of one species living in a habitat?
misconceptions.correct: No. That is a population. A community is the populations of all the different species living together in a habitat.
misconceptions.misconception: A community is all the members of one species that live together in a habitat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language a community is one group of similar people, so students carry that meaning across and apply it to a single species.
misconceptions.correction: The levels of organisation run from the individual organism, to the population of all the organisms of one species in a habitat, to the community of the populations of all the different species, to the whole ecosystem.

misconceptions.question: Are a predator and the prey it eats competing with each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Competition is between organisms that need the same limited resource. A new predator arriving is listed as a separate biotic factor that can affect a community.
misconceptions.misconception: Whenever one species harms another species, the two species must be competing with each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Competition is remembered as 'organisms fighting each other', so any harmful interaction between species, including one eating the other, gets labelled competition.
misconceptions.correction: Animals compete with each other for food, mates and territory, and plants compete for light and space, water and mineral ions, so competition is for the same limited resources. Biotic factors that can affect a community include availability of food, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and one species outcompeting another.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches a community in an ecosystem?

options.text: The populations of every species in a habitat
options.rationale: A community is the populations of all the different species living together in a habitat; the ecosystem is the interaction of that community with the non-living parts of the environment.

options.text: The individuals of one species in a habitat
options.rationale: A student who thinks a community is one group of similar organisms picks the single-species option. This is wrong because all the organisms of one species in a habitat form a population, and the community is made of the populations of all the different species.

options.text: The living and non-living parts of a habitat
options.rationale: A student who treats 'community' and 'ecosystem' as the same word picks the option that includes the non-living parts. This is wrong because the non-living (abiotic) parts belong to the ecosystem, which is the interaction of the community with them, not to the community itself.

options.text: The non-living conditions present in a habitat
options.rationale: A student who does not separate living factors from non-living ones picks the description of the abiotic conditions. This is wrong because those conditions are the abiotic factors, such as light intensity and temperature, while a community is made only of living organisms.

mcqs.stem: A gardener sows seedlings very close together in fertile, well-watered soil in an open bed. Which pair of resources will these plants mainly compete for as they grow?

options.text: Light and mineral ions in the soil
options.rationale: Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil, and crowded seedlings shade each other and draw on the same soil.

options.text: Food and territory around each plant
options.rationale: A student who believes plants compete for the same things as animals picks food and territory. This is wrong because those are things animals compete for; plants make their own food and compete for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil.

options.text: Mates and shelter from other plants
options.rationale: A student applying the animal list of resources to plants picks mates and shelter. This is wrong because mates are a resource animals compete for; plants in a community or habitat compete for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil.

options.text: Food and water taken up from the soil
options.rationale: A student who calls what a plant takes from the soil its 'food' picks this pair. Water is correct but food is not, because plants take up water and mineral ions from the soil and make their own food, so this option describes competition in animal terms.

mcqs.stem: A disease kills nearly all the insects that pollinate several plant species in a woodland. Which outcome best shows interdependence in this community?

options.text: Other woodland species are unaffected by it
options.rationale: A student who thinks a change stays with the species it hits picks this. It is wrong because within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal, so removing one species can affect the whole community.

options.text: Many other species in the woodland are affected
options.rationale: This is interdependence: each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc., so if one species is removed it can affect the whole community.

options.text: Plants are unaffected as they feed themselves
options.rationale: A student who believes plants making their own food makes them independent picks this. It is wrong because organisms require materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there, and these plants depend on the insects for pollination.

options.text: Nothing changes as the community is stable
options.rationale: A student who reads 'stable' as 'unchanging' picks this. It is wrong because a stable community is one where the species and environmental factors are in balance so population sizes stay fairly constant; losing a species removes that balance.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a stable community?

options.text: Population sizes remain exactly the same each year
options.rationale: A student who reads 'stable' as 'fixed' picks exactly the same numbers. This is wrong because in a stable community population sizes remain fairly constant, rising and falling around an average rather than staying identical.

options.text: The species stop competing for food and territory
options.rationale: A student who thinks balance means nothing is happening picks the end of competition. This is wrong because animals go on competing for food, mates and territory in a stable community; it is the balance of species and environmental factors that keeps numbers fairly constant.

options.text: Species and environmental factors are in balance
options.rationale: A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.

options.text: The abiotic factors in this habitat remain constant
options.rationale: A student who extends 'nothing changes' to the surroundings picks unchanging abiotic factors. This is wrong because abiotic factors such as temperature and light intensity vary; a stable community requires species and environmental factors to be in balance, not frozen.

mcqs.stem:
The table shows the mean number of mayfly nymphs collected at four sites along one river.

Site | Dissolved oxygen in mg/dm3 | Mean number of nymphs per sample
W | 9.8 | 42
X | 8.1 | 35
Y | 5.4 | 12
Z | 3.2 | 2

Which conclusion about an abiotic factor is supported by these data?

options.text: Dissolved oxygen is a biotic factor for the nymphs
options.rationale: A student who labels any outside influence as living picks this. It is wrong because oxygen levels for aquatic animals are listed as an abiotic (non-living) factor; biotic factors are things such as food availability, new predators and new pathogens.

options.text: Nymph numbers are constant in the whole river
options.rationale: A student who assumes a community in balance has constant numbers ignores the figures. It is wrong because the table shows numbers falling from 42 at site W to 2 at site Z, so they are not constant along the river.

options.text: Other river species are unaffected by low oxygen
options.rationale: A student who thinks a change affects only the species measured picks this. It is wrong because the table gives no data on other species, and species in a community depend on each other, so a change can affect the whole community.

options.text: Fewer nymphs were found where oxygen was lower
options.rationale: The data show the mean number of nymphs falling from 42 to 2 as dissolved oxygen falls from 9.8 to 3.2 mg/dm3, so this abiotic factor, oxygen levels for aquatic animals, is linked to the size of the population.

mcqs.stem:
The table shows the numbers of a predator and of its prey counted in the same community over four years.

Year | Number of prey | Number of predators
1 | 1200 | 30
2 | 900 | 45
3 | 600 | 60
4 | 800 | 40

Which statement is best supported by these data?

options.text: Predators and prey compete for the same food
options.rationale: A student who treats any harmful interaction as competition picks this. It is wrong because the predator eats the prey, and the table gives no data on their food sources; competition is between organisms needing the same limited resource.

options.text: Numbers stayed constant in a stable community
options.rationale: A student who reads 'stable' as 'unchanging' picks this. It is wrong because the figures change every year; in a stable community population sizes remain fairly constant while still rising and falling.

options.text: Other species were unaffected by the change
options.rationale: A student who limits the effect to the two species in the table picks this. It is wrong because no other species were counted, and each species depends on others, so a change can affect the whole community.

options.text: Prey numbers fell as predator numbers rose
options.rationale: From year 1 to year 3 the prey fell from 1200 to 600 while the predators rose from 30 to 60, and in year 4 the prey rose as the predators fell, showing how a change in a biotic factor affects the community.

mcqs.stem: Rats reach an island on a ship and begin to eat the eggs of a ground-nesting bird. Which biotic factor does this describe?

options.text: One species outcompeting another species
options.rationale: A student who calls every harmful interaction competition picks outcompeting. It is wrong because the rats eat the eggs rather than using up a resource the birds need, so this is a new predator arriving, not one species outcompeting another.

options.text: A new predator arriving in this community
options.rationale: New predators arriving is one of the biotic (living) factors which can affect a community, and the rats are feeding on the birds' eggs.

options.text: A drop in the soil's moisture levels
options.rationale: A student who does not separate living from non-living factors picks a soil condition. It is wrong because moisture levels are an abiotic factor, while the arrival of the rats is a living, biotic factor.

options.text: A change in the temperature of this island
options.rationale: A student who treats any outside change as environmental and non-living picks temperature. It is wrong because temperature is listed as an abiotic factor; the rats are living organisms, so they are a biotic factor.

mcqs.stem: Camels live in hot deserts. Which of these is a behavioural adaptation of a camel to desert conditions?

options.text: It has thick fat stored in a hump on its back
options.rationale: A student who thinks all adaptations are body features picks the hump. It is an adaptation, but a structural one, because it is a feature of the camel's body rather than something the camel does.

options.text: It makes small amounts of concentrated urine
options.rationale: A student who does not separate the three types of adaptation picks this. It is an adaptation, but a functional one, because it describes the way a process inside the camel's body works.

options.text: It rests in the shade during the hottest hours
options.rationale: Adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional, and resting in shade is something the camel does, so it is a behavioural adaptation that helps it survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

options.text: It has long eyelashes to keep out the sand
options.rationale: A student who expects adaptations to be visible body parts picks the eyelashes. It is an adaptation, but a structural one, because it is a feature of the camel's body, not a way the camel behaves.

mcqs.stem: Bacteria that live in deep sea vents are described as extremophiles. Why?

options.text: They live in seawater that is warmer than average
options.rationale: A student who thinks any warm habitat counts picks this. It is wrong because extremophiles live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration, not merely above average conditions.

options.text: They survive by moving away from the hottest water
options.rationale: A student who thinks extremophiles escape the conditions picks this. It is wrong because extremophiles live in the extreme environment itself; that is what makes them extremophiles.

options.text: They tolerate the extreme heat for short periods
options.rationale: A student who confuses briefly enduring conditions with living in them picks this. It is wrong because extremophiles normally live in the very extreme environment rather than visiting it for short periods.

options.text: They live in water of extreme heat and pressure
options.rationale: Some organisms live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration, and these organisms are called extremophiles; bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.
